title: The 3+1 and 2+2 formalisms
one_line_summary: Rebuilds the Cauchy problem of Chapter 13 geometrically: a spacelike hypersurface is described by its induced metric and extrinsic curvature, the Gauss, Codazzi and Ricci equations recover spacetime curvature from them, a foliation plus lapse and shift turns vacuum Einstein equations into four constraints and first-order evolution equations for (gamma, K), numerical-relativity practice (conformal initial data, slicing and shift gauges) is surveyed, and the 2+2 double-foliation alternative is sketched with its lapse matrix, two shifts and conformal 2-structure.
role_in_book: Chapter 13 showed in special coordinates that Einstein's equations split into constraints and evolution equations and argued existence via Cauchy-Kowalevskaya. Chapter 14 is the coordinate-free, geometric sequel: it supplies the machinery (projection operators, induced connection, extrinsic curvature, Lie derivatives along the normal) that numerical relativity actually uses and that underlies the ADM Hamiltonian picture of 'geometrodynamics'. It closes the 'structure of the field equations' block before the book turns to exact solutions in Chapter 15 (whose spherically symmetric metric already appears in Exercise 14.4), and the 2+2 and characteristic sections plant the null-hypersurface ideas that Chapter 23 (Bondi's radiating metric, characteristic initial value problem) develops. In style it is markedly more differential-geometric than the book's early chapters, and its further reading says the ordering follows Gourgoulhon's lecture notes.

assumed_background.topic: Tensor fields, index notation, contraction, raising/lowering with the metric
Lie derivative of tensors along a vector field and its expression with a torsion-free covariant derivative
Affine connection, covariant differentiation, torsion, and the uniqueness of the metric (Levi-Civita) connection
Riemann tensor as the commutator of covariant derivatives, its symmetries, Ricci tensor and scalar
Einstein tensor, vacuum field equations, contracted Bianchi identities
Cauchy problem for Einstein's equations: constraints versus evolution equations, role of g_{0a}, Cauchy-Kowalevskaya theorem
Metric signature (+,-,-,-), timelike/spacelike/null vectors, proper time along worldlines
Tensor densities and the metric determinant (for the ADM momentum and conformal factor)
Hamiltonian/Lagrangian mechanics: generalized coordinates, velocities, conjugate momenta, degrees of freedom
Classification of PDEs (elliptic versus hyperbolic), well-posed initial value problems
Classical surface theory: first and second fundamental forms of a surface in Euclidean space

learning_objectives: Reader can build the projection operator B_a^b from the unit normal of a spacelike hypersurface and prove it is idempotent and annihilates the normal.
Reader can define the induced metric h_ab = g_ab - n_a n_b, explain why its spatial part is negative definite in the (+,-,-,-) signature, and pass to the positive definite gamma_ab = -h_ab.
Reader can define the induced covariant derivative by double projection and argue that it is the Levi-Civita connection of h_ab.

Reader can define the extrinsic curvature as minus the doubly projected gradient of the unit normal, show it is symmetric and tangential, and interpret it as the normal part of the spacetime derivative of tangent fields (the Gauss formula).
Reader can state the Gauss, Codazzi and Ricci equations, say which projections of the Riemann tensor each one supplies, and explain why the Ricci equation needs a foliation.
Reader can contract the Gauss and Codazzi equations to obtain the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints and explain why these contain no normal time derivatives.
Reader can define a foliation by a time function, the lapse N, the Eulerian observer, and prove that N = d tau / d t.
Reader can derive K_ab = -(1/2) L_n h_ab and the acceleration relation A_a = -D_a ln N.
Reader can decompose a rigging vector T = N n + beta into lapse and shift and write the 3+1 line element and inverse metric in adapted coordinates.
Reader can write the vacuum ADM evolution equations for gamma_{mu nu} and K_{mu nu}, identify lapse and shift as non-dynamical gauge functions, and outline the constrain-then-evolve procedure.
Reader can summarize the York-O Murchadha conformal method for solving the constraints and the simplifications from conformal flatness, maximal slicing and vanishing TT data.
Reader can compare slicing conditions (geodesic, Lagrangian, maximal) and shift conditions (Eulerian, Lagrangian, isothermal, radial) in terms of singularity avoidance and simplicity.
Reader can reproduce the counting argument that reduces 10 metric functions to 2 gravitational degrees of freedom.

Reader can describe the 2+2 construction (two transvecting vector fields, double-null and null-timelike foliations), the lapse matrix N_AB, the two shift vectors, and the conformal 2-structure as carrier of the free data.

teaching_approach.summary: Geometry-before-coordinates, following Gourgoulhon: the authors first study one hypersurface in isolation (intrinsic and extrinsic geometry, Gauss-Codazzi), then add a family of hypersurfaces (foliation, acceleration, Ricci equation, lapse), and only then add a threading congruence (rigging vector, shift) that produces coordinates and PDEs. Each layer is introduced exactly when the previous layer cannot supply the next curvature component or time derivative. Derivations are fully index-explicit with projection operators, with many small steps left as exercises, and results are restated in adapted coordinates using the starred equality. The later sections switch register to a literature survey (numerical relativity gauges, conformal data) and to an author-driven overview of the 2+2 formalism, where only the metric decomposition is done in detail.
narrative_arc: Motivating problem: Chapter 13 did the Cauchy problem in special coordinates; can the same split be phrased geometrically, as data living on a slice?
Model one spacelike hypersurface: unit normal, projection operator, induced metric, sign flip to a positive definite 3-metric.
Intrinsic calculus: induced covariant derivative by double projection, proved to be the metric connection of h_ab.
Extrinsic data: define K_ab from the tangential derivative of the normal, show symmetry, and package the tangential/normal split of nabla_Y X.

Reconstruction question: how much spacetime curvature do (gamma, K) determine? State Gauss and Codazzi, contract them to the two constraint equations, then prove both in separate calculational sections.

Add a family of slices: Cauchy surfaces and global hyperbolicity justify M = Sigma x R; the normal can now be differentiated off the slice, giving the acceleration and the Ricci equation for the last curvature component.
Introduce the time function and lapse; interpret N as proper time per coordinate time via an Eulerian observer; show K is minus half the normal Lie derivative of h.
Relax the normal-observer restriction: arbitrary threading curves give the rigging vector, decomposed into lapse and shift; derive the 3+1 metric and line element.
Dynamics: project G_ab = 0 three ways, convert L_n into L_T = partial_t, and obtain first-order evolution equations for (gamma, K) plus four constraints; lapse and shift carry no evolution equation.
Procedure and history: solve constraints, pick gauge, evolve; constraints are preserved by Bianchi identities; Darmois, Lichnerowicz, Choquet-Bruhat, ADM.
Application survey: conformal-TT construction of initial data and the menu of slicing and shift conditions used in numerical codes.

Critique and alternative: 3+1 hides the two true degrees of freedom and breaks down on null slices; counting argument; 2+2 double foliation with lapse matrix, two shifts and conformal 2-structure; pointer to Bondi's metric in Chapter 23.
signature_moves: Projection-operator bookkeeping: every hypersurface object is manufactured by sandwiching a spacetime object between copies of B_a^b, and the identities B n = 0 and B B = B do almost all the work in the long derivations.
Layered geometry: single hypersurface, then foliation, then fibration, each layer unlocking exactly one new ingredient (K, then A and the Ricci equation, then shift and coordinates).
Starred equality (*=) to flag results that hold only in adapted coordinates, keeping the covariant statement and its coordinate shadow side by side.
Announce the key equations first (Gauss 14.23, Codazzi 14.25, Ricci 14.53) and extract their physics (the constraints) before proving them in dedicated calculation sections.
Physical reading of formal objects via observers: the normal as an observer's 4-velocity, A^a as that observer's acceleration, the lapse as proper time elapsed per tick of coordinate time.
Comparative metric decompositions: the 2+2 contravariant and covariant metrics are laid out as block matrices explicitly to be compared line by line with the 3+1 ones.
Degree-of-freedom accounting as a narrative device to motivate a better formalism (2+2) rather than as an isolated fact.
Frequent 'exercise' and 'check' markers inside derivations, turning the text into a guided calculation that the exercise list then completes.

sections.title: The geometry of submanifolds
sections.summary: A one-page roadmap. It announces that the chapter redoes the Cauchy problem geometrically: embed a hypersurface, identify the induced metric and extrinsic curvature as the data that rebuild spacetime curvature, slice spacetime with a time function (foliation, lapse), thread it with timelike curves (fibration, shift), and read Einstein's equations as first-order evolution of (metric, extrinsic curvature). It names ADM (1959) and Wheeler's geometrodynamics and previews the 2+2 approach for null data and explicit degrees of freedom.
key_moves: Frames lapse and shift as the four free functions matching the fourfold coordinate freedom.
Positions GR as a dynamical system with dynamical variables (h, K) evolving in a time function.

sections.title: The induced metric
sections.summary: For a spacelike hypersurface with future-pointing unit timelike normal (n.n = +1 in this signature), the operator delta minus n n projects spacetime vectors and covectors into the surface; it kills the normal and squares to itself. Projecting g gives the induced metric h = g - n n, which agrees with g on tangent vectors. In coordinates where the surface is t = 0, h_{alpha beta} are just the spatial components of g and have signature (-,-,-), so the book introduces the positive definite gamma = -h.
concepts: unit normal to a spacelike hypersurface
key_moves: Verify tangency of B X by contracting with n.
Derive h_ab = g_ab - n_a n_b from the double projection.
Flip the sign to gamma_ab = -h_ab because of the (+,-,-,-) signature.

sections.title: The induced covariant derivative
sections.summary: Extend a tangent field off the surface, take the tangential derivative (independent of the extension), and project the free index back into the surface to define D_a; the same recipe works on any tensor. D annihilates h and is torsion-free, so it is the Levi-Civita derivative of h (and of gamma). In adapted coordinates the spatial 4D Christoffel symbols equal the 3D ones. The normal component of the tangential derivative defines the extrinsic curvature K_ab = -B B nabla n, which is tangential and symmetric, and the full split nabla_Y X = D_Y X + K(X,Y) n follows.
key_moves: Show D_e h_ab = 0 using B n = 0.
Invoke uniqueness of the torsion-free metric-compatible connection.
Use n.X = 0 to move the derivative from X onto n, defining K.
Split Y.nabla X into tangential (D) and normal (K) parts, eq. (14.21).

sections.title: The Gauss-Codazzi equations
sections.summary: States (proofs deferred) the Gauss equation, which gives the fully tangential projection of the Riemann tensor as 3D curvature plus quadratic K terms, and the Codazzi equation, which gives the three-tangential-one-normal projection as antisymmetrized D K. Together these give every Riemann component except R_{alpha 0 beta 0}, which needs normal derivatives of n and hence a foliation. Contracting Gauss twice yields G_ab n^a n^b in terms of (3)R and K (the Hamiltonian constraint); contracting Codazzi yields the mixed projection of G (the momentum constraint). Both involve only the slice data and their tangential derivatives, so they constrain initial data.
key_moves: Use g^{ac} = h^{ac} + n^a n^c to contract the Gauss equation.
Contract a second time and match against the normal-normal Einstein component, which is the normal-normal Ricci component minus half the scalar curvature.
Contract Codazzi on a and c to reach B n G.
Remark on whether the contractions can be done with gamma instead of h (see gaps: this remark is not correct for the (3)R term).

sections.title: Calculating the Gauss equation
sections.summary: Start from the 3D Ricci identity for a tangent field Z, expand D_a D_b Z by writing each D as projected nabla, and differentiate the projectors themselves. Derivatives of B produce n times K, so after antisymmetrizing in a and b one term drops out and the rest leave the projected 4D commutator plus two K K products. Replacing Z by the projection of an arbitrary field and stripping it gives the Gauss equation.
key_moves: Differentiate the projector: only its n n part contributes, giving two terms each carrying one derivative of the normal (14.37).
Show the projected derivative of B equals n^d K_ab (14.38) and n_c K_a^c (14.39).
Use n.Z = 0 to trade n_e nabla Z^e for Z^e K_eb (14.41).
Antisymmetrize and strip the arbitrary vector.

sections.title: Calculating the Codazzi equation
sections.summary: Differentiate K_ab = -B B nabla n with the projected derivative, expand the product rule over the projectors, observe that the two projector-derivative terms are symmetric under a<->c and cancel on antisymmetrization, and recognize the remaining commutator of 4D derivatives acting on n as the Riemann tensor contracted with n.
key_moves: Apply the definition (14.13) of D to K.
Cancel terms symmetric in the antisymmetrized pair.
Replace the commutator acting on n_k by Riemann contracted with n.

sections.title: The geometry of foliations
sections.summary: Defines a Cauchy surface (met exactly once by every endless causal curve) and global hyperbolicity, whose key consequence is the product topology M = Sigma x R. A foliation is the family of level sets of a scalar with nowhere-vanishing gradient, filling M without intersection. With a family of spacelike slices the normal can be differentiated along itself, giving the acceleration A = nabla_n n of normal observers, which is orthogonal to n. The Ricci equation, supplying the last curvature projection n R n, is stated in terms of L_n K, D A, A A and K K.
key_moves: Motivate foliations from the topology theorem for globally hyperbolic spacetimes.
Differentiate n.n = 1 to show A is spatial.
Identify A as the new datum needed for R_{alpha 0 beta 0}.

sections.title: Derivation of the Ricci equation
sections.summary: With A in hand, the full gradient of the normal is nabla_a n_b = -K_ab + n_a A_b. Expanding L_n K with this decomposition, rewriting n.nabla K through second derivatives of n, and splitting nabla A into D A plus normal pieces, all normal-index terms cancel and the commutator of derivatives on n becomes Riemann contracted twice with n. The result is the Ricci equation, a purely tangential tensor identity.
concepts: decomposition of the gradient of the normal
key_moves: Establish nabla_a n_b = -K_ab + n_a A_b (14.54).
Write L_n K with the torsion-free formula (14.55).
Combine (14.57)-(14.59) and cancel the n_a A^c K terms.
Use symmetries of Riemann to show n n R is tangential.

sections.title: The lapse function
sections.summary: When the gradient of the scalar is timelike the scalar is a time function t; the normal is N times the raised gradient, and the lapse N = 1/sqrt(g^{ab} t_a t_b) is positive. The Eulerian observer (worldline along n) regards each slice as simultaneous. Stepping a proper time d tau along n moves to the slice t + d tau/N, so N = d tau/dt. The normal Lie derivative of h equals -2K, giving K = -(1/2) L_n h and, in coordinates carried by Eulerian observers, gamma-dot = 2 N K. The acceleration is minus the spatial gradient of ln N, which simplifies the Ricci equation; combined with the contracted Gauss equation it becomes an evolution equation for K.
concepts: extrinsic curvature as rate of change of the induced metric
evolution equation for the extrinsic curvature
key_moves: Taylor-expand t along the normal to get N = d tau/dt (14.67).
Compute L_n g and L_n(n n) to get L_n h = -2K (14.71).
Use n = (1/N) partial_t in Eulerian-adapted coordinates for gamma-dot = 2NK.
Show D A - A A = -(1/N) D D N and substitute into the Ricci equation.
Swap n n Riemann for projected Ricci via the contracted Gauss equation (14.77).

sections.title: The 3+1 decomposition of the metric
sections.summary: Normal observers are too restrictive, so any congruence of curves transverse to the slices (a fibration) is allowed. Its t-parametrized tangent T, the rigging vector, splits into a normal part (the lapse N, fixed by the foliation) and a tangential part, the shift beta. Coordinates constant along the threading curves make T = partial_t. Substituting into g^{ab} = h^{ab} + n n gives the block form of the inverse metric, inversion gives the covariant metric, and hence the 3+1 line element. The inverse metric's spatial block is -gamma^{mu nu} only when the shift vanishes.
key_moves: Split T = N n + beta with N = T.n, beta = B T (14.78).
Express n = (T - beta)/N and substitute into the inverse metric (14.82).
Use T^a *= delta^a_0 to read off components (14.87).
Invert with the determinant relation det gamma^{mu nu} = -N^2 det g^{ab} (14.89)-(14.90).

sections.title: The 3+1 decomposition of the vacuum Einstein equations
sections.summary: Recasts GR as the time history of a 3-geometry: lapse and shift (four functions) are freely chosen kinematical data, the six components of gamma are dynamical. G_ab = 0 is projected normal-normal (Hamiltonian constraint), normal-tangential (momentum constraint), and tangential-tangential (conveniently using R_ab = 0). The Ricci-equation result gives L_n K; L_n h = -2K gives the metric's evolution. Converting to L_T (partial_t in adapted coordinates) splits each Lie derivative into an N-scaled normal part and a shift Lie derivative expressed with D, yielding first-order PDEs for gamma_{mu nu} and K_{mu nu}. The Cauchy procedure, preservation of constraints by the Bianchi identities, the history from Darmois to ADM (with p^{ab}), and the difficulty of existence proofs for non-analytic data close the section.
key_moves: Project Einstein's equations into three pieces, using R_ab for the spatial projection.
Show L_{Nn} h = N L_n h because n.h = 0 kills the gradient-of-N terms.
Expand L_beta with D because beta is tangent and D h = 0.
Solve (14.102) for K to get (14.103), making the system second order in gamma.
Stress that N and beta have no evolution equations and correspond to g_{0a} in Chapter 13.

sections.title: The 3+1 equations and numerical relativity
sections.summary: A quoted-results survey. Initial data: the York-O Murchadha conformal approach writes gamma = psi^4 gamma-hat, splits K into trace and trace-free parts, scales the trace-free part by psi^-10, decomposes it into a transverse-traceless piece plus a conformal-Killing-type derivative of a vector potential, and turns the constraints into four coupled quasilinear elliptic equations for psi and X. Flat conformal metric, maximal slice and zero TT data decouple and linearize the momentum constraint, enabling analytic black-hole data with chosen momenta and spins. Gauge: lapse choices (geodesic and Lagrangian slicing are singularity seeking; maximal slicing avoids focusing at the cost of an elliptic solve) and shift choices (Eulerian, Lagrangian with grid distortion, isothermal and radial gauges that zero metric components).
key_moves: Choose conformal weights (psi^4 on gamma, psi^-10 on the trace-free K) so the divergence scales simply (14.112).
Reverse-decompose the TT part so the free data is an arbitrary traceless symmetric T-hat.
List the three free-data choices that decouple the system.
Tie lapse choice to singularity avoidance and shift choice to simplicity of the equations.

sections.title: The 2+2 and characteristic approaches
sections.summary: Two limitations of 3+1 motivate an alternative: the free data are hidden behind constraints, and spacelike slicing fails on null surfaces. A counting argument reduces ten metric components to four data (two configuration and two velocity), i.e. two degrees of freedom, but 3+1 never exhibits them and carries six evolution equations. The 2+2 approach starts from a spacelike 2-surface and two transvecting vector fields that drag it into two families of 3-surfaces; if both are null one gets a double-null foliation, if one is null and one timelike a null-timelike foliation. Advantages: the conformal 2-geometry carries the two degrees of freedom, the free data are unconstrained and obey ODEs along the vector fields, and null and characteristic initial value problems (radiation, null infinity, cosmological past light cones) are handled naturally.
key_moves: Pose the two questions: which are the free data, and why six evolution equations?
Construct foliations by dragging an initial 2-surface along two vector fields.
List the physical arenas where null data are natural.

sections.title: The 2+2 metric decomposition
sections.summary: Two scalar functions define intersecting hypersurface families whose intersections are spacelike 2-surfaces S(u, v). Their normal covectors give a dual dyad n_A spanning the orthogonal 2-space {T}, which is generally not integrable because the dyad's Lie bracket need not vanish. The Gram matrix N_AB of the dyad is the orthogonal 2-metric in dyad components and generalizes the lapse; projectors onto {S} and {T} are built from the dyad. Connecting vectors E_A = n_A + b_A with arbitrary shifts b_A can always be chosen to commute, giving coordinates (x^0, x^1, x^2, x^3). The contravariant and covariant metrics then take block forms with a 2x2 lapse matrix and two shift vectors, compared explicitly with the 3+1 forms. Extracting the determinant of the 2-metric isolates the conformal 2-structure, which carries the two degrees of freedom; the Bondi-type coordinates of Chapter 23 are previewed.
key_moves: Define dual dyads with n^A_a n_B^a = delta^A_B.
Note [n_0, n_1] != 0 generically, so {T} is not surface-forming.
Use freedom in b_A to make [E_0, E_1] = 0 and adopt coordinates along E_A.
Read off block matrices (14.138)-(14.139).
Divide out the area element to get the conformal 2-structure.

sections.title: Exercises and further reading
sections.summary: Twelve exercises complete the gaps flagged in the text (projector identities, torsion-freeness of D, the contracted Gauss relation, the gradient of the normal, L_n(n n), gamma-dot = 2NK, A = -D ln N, the K evolution equation, and the 2+2 metric blocks), plus one concrete slice computation for a time-dependent spherically symmetric metric. Further reading points to Smarr (1979) and Gourgoulhon (2012) for 3+1, warns about signature-driven sign differences in numerical-relativity texts, and to d'Inverno (1996), d'Inverno-Smallwood (1980), d'Inverno-Stachel (1978) and Brady et al. (1996) for 2+2.
key_moves: Exercises are keyed to sections and fill the '(exercise)' markers in derivations.
Explicit warning that (-,+,+,+) numerical-relativity literature differs in signs.

concepts.name: spacelike hypersurface
concepts.definition: A three-dimensional submanifold of spacetime all of whose tangent vectors are spacelike; equivalently its normal is timelike.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken as the arena on which initial data live, as the geometric replacement for the t = 0 surface of Chapter 13's coordinate treatment.

concepts.name: unit normal to a spacelike hypersurface
concepts.definition: The future-directed timelike vector field orthogonal to every tangent vector of the hypersurface, normalized so that n_a n^a = +1 in the (+,-,-,-) signature.
concepts.how_introduced: First object constructed for a hypersurface; later reinterpreted as the 4-velocity of Eulerian observers.

concepts.name: projection operator onto a hypersurface
concepts.definition: The mixed tensor B_a^b = delta_a^b - n_a n^b, which removes the normal component of any vector or covector; it annihilates n and is idempotent.
concepts.how_introduced: Built immediately from the normal and verified to produce tangent vectors; it is then the workhorse for defining every induced object by sandwiching.
prerequisites: unit normal to a spacelike hypersurface
concepts.notes: In the 2+2 section the same letter B denotes the projector onto the 2-surfaces.

concepts.name: induced metric
concepts.definition: The metric that the spacetime metric induces on the hypersurface, h_ab = B_a^c B_b^d g_cd = g_ab - n_a n_b; it agrees with g on pairs of tangent vectors.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by projecting g; in adapted coordinates shown to be simply the spatial block g_{alpha beta}.

concepts.name: positive definite spatial metric gamma
concepts.definition: In the (+,-,-,-) signature the induced metric is negative definite, so the book defines gamma_ab = -h_ab to work with a positive definite Riemannian metric on the slice.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced right after noting h_{alpha beta} has signature (-,-,-); the ADM variables are then written in terms of gamma.
concepts.notes: Christoffel symbols and Riemann R^a_{bcd} and Ricci R_ab are unchanged by h -> -h, but the Ricci scalar and any single contraction with the inverse metric change sign; see gaps_and_pitfalls.

concepts.name: adapted coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates (t, x^1, x^2, x^3) in which the hypersurface (or each leaf) is t = constant and the x^alpha are coordinates on it; results valid only in such charts are marked with a starred equals sign.
concepts.how_introduced: Used after each covariant result to show its component form, e.g. h_{alpha beta} equals g_{alpha beta} and the 4D and 3D Christoffel symbols agree.

concepts.name: induced covariant derivative
concepts.definition: For tensor fields tangent to the hypersurface, D_a is the spacetime covariant derivative with every index (including the derivative index) projected into the hypersurface; it depends only on the field on the surface.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in two steps: tangential derivative (independent of extension) followed by projecting the free index back into the surface, then generalized to arbitrary tangent tensors.

concepts.name: Levi-Civita connection uniqueness
concepts.definition: There is exactly one torsion-free covariant derivative that annihilates a given (pseudo-)metric; its coefficients are the Christoffel symbols of that metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked to conclude that D is the metric derivative of h, after showing D h = 0 and that D is torsion-free (the latter left as Exercise 14.3).

concepts.name: extrinsic curvature
concepts.definition: The symmetric tangential tensor obtained by projecting both indices of the spacetime gradient of the unit normal into the hypersurface and changing sign; it measures how the unit normal changes as one moves along the hypersurface, i.e. how the hypersurface bends inside spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Arises as the normal component of the tangential derivative of a tangent vector field, after moving the derivative onto n using n.X = 0; later re-expressed as minus half the normal Lie derivative of h when a foliation exists.
prerequisites: unit normal to a spacelike hypersurface
concepts.notes: Sign convention: with this definition, n future pointing and signature (+,-,-,-); numerical-relativity texts in (-,+,+,+) use K_ij = -(1/2) L_n gamma_ij, which is the negative of the book's K.

concepts.name: symmetry of the extrinsic curvature
concepts.definition: The extrinsic curvature of a hypersurface is a symmetric tensor, a consequence of the torsion-free spacetime connection together with the hypersurface-orthogonality of n.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted in one line from torsion-freeness; a learner should note that it uses the fact that n is normal to a family of surfaces or, for a single surface, that commutators of tangent fields stay tangent (Exercise 14.3(i)).

concepts.name: Gauss formula for covariant derivatives
concepts.definition: For vector fields tangent to a hypersurface, the spacetime derivative of X along Y equals the intrinsic derivative D_Y X plus K(X,Y) times the unit normal.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as an alternative, very useful reading of K: the part of the 4D derivative that sticks out of the surface.

concepts.name: Ricci identity (commutator of covariant derivatives)
concepts.definition: The antisymmetrized second covariant derivative of a vector equals the Riemann tensor acting on it; applied both to D on the slice and to nabla in spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the starting point of both the Gauss and Codazzi derivations.
formulas: D_a D_b Z^c - D_b D_a Z^c = {}^{(3)}R^c{}_{dab} Z^d

concepts.name: Gauss equation
concepts.definition: The fully tangential projection of the spacetime Riemann tensor equals the intrinsic Riemann tensor of the hypersurface plus terms quadratic in the extrinsic curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced as the first reconstruction result, then proved in §14.5 by expanding the 3D Ricci identity with projected derivatives.
formulas: B_a{}^e B_b{}^f B_c{}^g B_d{}^h R_{efgh} = {}^{(3)}R_{abcd} + K_{ad}K_{bc} - K_{ac}K_{bd}

concepts.name: Codazzi equation
concepts.definition: The projection of the spacetime Riemann tensor with three indices tangent to the hypersurface and one along the normal equals an antisymmetrized intrinsic derivative of the extrinsic curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced with Gauss, proved in §14.6 by differentiating K and antisymmetrizing.
formulas: B_a{}^e B_b{}^f B_c{}^g n^h R_{efgh} = D_b K_{ac} - D_a K_{bc}

concepts.name: constraint equations
concepts.definition: The four components G_ab n^a n^b and B_a^c n^d G_cd of Einstein's equations, which involve only the induced metric, extrinsic curvature and their tangential derivatives, and so restrict which data may be posed on a slice.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by contracting the Gauss and Codazzi equations; linked back to the constraints found in coordinates in §13.6.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian constraint
concepts.definition: The normal-normal projection of the vacuum Einstein equations, relating the scalar curvature of the slice to quadratic invariants of the extrinsic curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the twice-contracted Gauss equation; its name is explained later by the ADM Hamiltonian formulation.
concepts.notes: As printed, (3)R and all traces are computed with h. If gamma is used instead, (3)R changes sign and the standard form (3)R + K^2 - K_ab K^ab = 0 results.

concepts.name: momentum constraint
concepts.definition: The mixed normal-tangential projection of the vacuum Einstein equations, requiring the divergence of the extrinsic curvature to equal the gradient of its trace.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by contracting the Codazzi equation once; named after its role in ADM's Hamiltonian formulation.

concepts.name: Cauchy surface
concepts.definition: A spacelike hypersurface met exactly once by every endless timelike or null curve.
concepts.how_introduced: Opens the foliation section with a sketch (Fig. 14.1) of worldlines crossing a slice once.

concepts.name: global hyperbolicity
concepts.definition: The property of possessing a Cauchy surface; it guarantees unique global solutions of the wave equation and implies the manifold is a product of a 3-manifold with the real line.
concepts.how_introduced: Named via the hyperbolic wave equation and used to justify slicing spacetime into level surfaces of a time function.
concepts.notes: The product-topology result is quoted without proof or attribution (it is Geroch's theorem, later refined by Bernal and Sanchez).

concepts.name: foliation
concepts.definition: A decomposition of spacetime into non-intersecting level sets of a smooth scalar with nowhere-vanishing gradient, so each event lies on exactly one leaf.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced after global hyperbolicity; drawn as a stack of wavy sheets (Fig. 14.2); allows derivatives of the normal off a single slice.

concepts.name: time function
concepts.definition: A scalar field on spacetime whose gradient is everywhere timelike (future directed after raising), so its level sets are spacelike slices.
concepts.how_introduced: Specialization of the foliation scalar once the leaves are required to be spacelike.

concepts.name: acceleration of normal observers
aliases: geodesic curvature of the normal curves
concepts.definition: The vector A^a = n^b nabla_b n^a, the 4-acceleration of observers moving along the unit normal; it is orthogonal to n and vanishes exactly when the normal curves are geodesics.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the new object made possible by a foliation, since n can now be differentiated along itself; identified as the missing ingredient for the last curvature projection.
prerequisites: unit normal to a spacelike hypersurface

concepts.name: decomposition of the gradient of the normal
concepts.definition: For a foliation the full spacetime gradient of the unit normal splits into minus the extrinsic curvature plus the normal times the acceleration.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived (as Exercise 14.7) by inserting delta = B + n n on each index; it is the key substitution in the Ricci-equation and L_n h calculations.

concepts.name: Lie derivative
concepts.definition: The derivative of a tensor field along the flow of a vector field; with a torsion-free connection it can be written using covariant derivatives with extra terms involving derivatives of the vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Relied on from Chapter 6 to express rates of change of h and K along the normal and along the rigging vector; L_T becomes partial_t in adapted coordinates.

concepts.name: Ricci equation
concepts.definition: The projection of the spacetime Riemann tensor with two indices along the normal equals the normal Lie derivative of the extrinsic curvature plus acceleration and K-squared terms; it is the only curvature relation that requires a foliation.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated at the end of §14.7 as the answer to the missing R_{alpha 0 beta 0} component, derived in §14.8, simplified with the lapse in §14.9.
formulas: B_a{}^c n^d B_b{}^e n^f R_{cdef} = \mathcal{L}_n K_{ab} + D_a A_b - A_a A_b + K_a{}^c K_{cb}

concepts.name: lapse function
concepts.definition: The positive scalar relating the unit normal to the raised gradient of the time function; physically, the proper time an Eulerian observer ages per unit of coordinate time between neighbouring leaves.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined from n = N grad t, computed as 1/sqrt(g^{ab} t_a t_b), then interpreted via a small step along the normal (Fig. 14.3).
prerequisites: unit normal to a spacelike hypersurface
concepts.notes: The text switches between N and alpha for the lapse in §14.11-14.12.

concepts.name: Eulerian observer
concepts.definition: An observer whose worldline is an integral curve of the unit normal to the foliation, so that each leaf is a surface of simultaneity for them.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to give n a physical meaning and to interpret the lapse and acceleration.
prerequisites: unit normal to a spacelike hypersurface

concepts.name: extrinsic curvature as rate of change of the induced metric
concepts.definition: For a foliation, the extrinsic curvature equals minus one half of the Lie derivative of the induced metric along the unit normal, so in coordinates following Eulerian observers gamma-dot = 2 N K.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by expanding L_n(g - n n) with nabla g = 0 and the gradient decomposition; the book notes numerical relativists often take this as the definition, but it needs a foliation whereas the §14.3 definition needs only one surface.

concepts.name: evolution equation for the extrinsic curvature
concepts.definition: An equation giving the normal Lie derivative of K in terms of the projected spacetime Ricci tensor, the slice's Ricci tensor, K-quadratic terms, and the Hessian of the lapse divided by the lapse.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by substituting A = -D ln N into the Ricci equation and eliminating n n Riemann with the contracted Gauss equation.
formulas: \mathcal{L}_n K_{ab} = B_a{}^c B_b{}^d R_{cd} - {}^{(3)}R_{ab} + K_c{}^c K_{ab} + \tfrac{1}{N}D_a D_b N - 2K_{ac}K_b{}^c

concepts.name: fibration
concepts.definition: A congruence of curves, nowhere tangent to the leaves, with exactly one curve through each event; used to identify points on different leaves.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced because using only normal observers to build coordinates is physically and mathematically restrictive.

concepts.name: rigging vector
concepts.definition: The tangent vector T^a to the fibration curves parametrized by the time function, normalized so that moving a leaf by dt along T lands on the leaf t + dt; in adapted coordinates T = partial_t.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined from the fibration and immediately decomposed into normal and tangential parts (Fig. 14.4).

concepts.name: shift vector
concepts.definition: The part of the rigging vector tangent to the leaves; it measures how far the threading curve drifts sideways within the slice, relative to the normal, per unit coordinate time.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by projecting T into the slice; presented with the lapse as the four freely specifiable gauge functions.

concepts.name: 3+1 decomposition of the metric
aliases: lapse-shift form of the line element
concepts.definition: In coordinates adapted to a foliation and fibration, the spacetime metric is determined by the lapse, the shift and the spatial metric; the inverse metric and line element take block forms built from N, beta and gamma.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from g^{ab} = h^{ab} + n^a n^b by substituting n = (T - beta)/N, then inverted.
concepts.notes: The printed book has +beta^sigma beta_sigma in g_00 and -beta^mu/N in g^{0mu}; see gaps for why these appear to be misprints.

concepts.name: ADM evolution equations
concepts.definition: The first-order-in-time PDE system giving partial_t of the spatial metric in terms of lapse, extrinsic curvature and shift derivatives, and partial_t of the extrinsic curvature in terms of the Hessian of the lapse, shift Lie-derivative terms, the slice's Ricci tensor and K-quadratic terms.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by replacing L_n by L_T = L_{Nn} + L_beta, using n.h = 0 and n.K = 0 to drop gradient-of-N terms and D to expand shift terms.

concepts.notes: Signs of the shift terms and K-quadratic terms depend on whether indices are moved with h or gamma; the book is not consistent on this.

concepts.name: gauge freedom in the 3+1 split
concepts.definition: Lapse and shift obey no evolution equations; they are four arbitrary functions encoding how coordinates are laid down and correspond to the g_{0a} components that had to be specified in Chapter 13.
concepts.how_introduced: Emphasized after the evolution equations are obtained, and turned into practical gauge conditions in §14.12.

concepts.name: constraint propagation
aliases: preservation of constraints by Bianchi identities
concepts.definition: If the constraints hold on the initial slice and the evolution equations hold throughout, the contracted Bianchi identities guarantee the constraints continue to hold.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as part of the Cauchy procedure and again in the counting argument of §14.13.

concepts.name: canonical momentum conjugate to the 3-metric
concepts.definition: In the ADM Hamiltonian formulation the variable conjugate to the spatial metric, a density built from the trace-reversed extrinsic curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned historically to explain the names Hamiltonian and momentum constraint.

concepts.name: ADM formalism
concepts.definition: The 1959 Hamiltonian formulation of general relativity in terms of the spatial metric and its conjugate momentum, with lapse and shift as Lagrange multipliers enforcing the constraints.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the overview and in the history paragraph; the book's first-order system is presented as a close variant.

concepts.name: geometrodynamics
concepts.definition: Wheeler's view of general relativity as the evolution of the geometry of space through a sequence of spacelike slices.
concepts.how_introduced: Name-checked in the overview and echoed in §14.11 as the 'time history' of a slice.

concepts.name: well-posed initial value problem
concepts.definition: An initial value formulation whose solutions exist, are unique and depend continuously on data; for GR, proofs beyond analytic data need PDE theory rather than the Cauchy-Kowalevskaya theorem.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised at the end of §14.11 to contrast analytic existence (Darmois, Lichnerowicz) with the harder non-analytic case for which the 3+1 form is the starting point.

concepts.name: numerical relativity
concepts.definition: Solving Einstein's equations approximately on computers, typically by constructing constrained initial data and evolving the 3+1 system with chosen gauge conditions.
concepts.how_introduced: Section 14.12 surveys how the 3+1 equations are used, citing gravitational collapse and gravitational waves.

concepts.name: conformal method for initial data
concepts.definition: A way to solve the constraints by freely choosing a conformal 3-metric, the mean curvature and a traceless tensor, then solving four coupled elliptic equations for a conformal factor and a vector potential and rescaling back.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from the literature as the most useful route; summarized as a three-step recipe with a simplest-choice example.

concepts.name: conformal factor
concepts.definition: A positive scalar psi with gamma = psi^4 times a chosen background metric; the Hamiltonian constraint becomes an elliptic equation for psi.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the first of the four 'potentials', with the transformation law for the scalar curvature.

concepts.name: trace-free extrinsic curvature
concepts.definition: The extrinsic curvature minus one third of its trace times the metric; together with the trace K it carries all of K.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as the object to be conformally rescaled and TT-decomposed.

concepts.name: transverse-traceless decomposition
concepts.definition: The splitting of a symmetric traceless tensor into a divergence-free traceless (TT) part and a longitudinal part generated by a vector through the conformal Killing operator.
concepts.how_introduced: Used on the rescaled trace-free K, then 'reverse decomposed' so the free datum is an arbitrary traceless symmetric tensor.

concepts.name: conformal Killing operator
concepts.definition: The operator that maps a vector field W to the symmetric traceless tensor D^mu W^nu + D^nu W^mu - (2/3) gamma^{mu nu} D.W; its kernel consists of conformal Killing vectors, and its divergence is the vector Laplacian.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears inside the TT decomposition; its divergence defines the elliptic operator in the momentum constraint.

concepts.name: maximal slicing
concepts.definition: A slicing in which the trace of the extrinsic curvature vanishes on every leaf, enforced by solving an elliptic equation for the lapse; it prevents focusing of normal observers and so avoids singularities.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed as the singularity-avoiding lapse choice, with its elliptic lapse equation; also used as a simplifying choice for initial data.

concepts.name: geodesic slicing
concepts.definition: The gauge with unit lapse and zero shift, so coordinate observers are freely falling normal observers and slices are geodesically parallel; it tends to run into singularities.
concepts.how_introduced: First item in the lapse menu; also historically Darmois's 1927 case.
concepts.notes: The book puts 'Gaussian normal coordinates' in bold when it describes Darmois's 1927 case (p. 257): unit lapse, zero shift, slices labelled by the proper time of freely falling Eulerian observers.

concepts.name: Lagrangian slicing
concepts.definition: In spherical symmetry, choosing the lapse so that fluid worldlines are orthogonal to the slices and the zero-shift coordinates move with the matter; fluid worldlines focus toward singularities, so it is singularity seeking.
concepts.how_introduced: Second lapse option, with the condition N U^0 = 1.

concepts.name: singularity avoidance
concepts.definition: The practical requirement that the lapse slow down evolution in regions approaching a singularity so that the numerical slices do not hit it.
concepts.how_introduced: The first motivation offered for choosing gauge conditions, used to classify slicings.

concepts.name: shift gauge conditions
concepts.definition: Rules fixing the shift: zero shift (Eulerian); shift equal to the fluid 3-velocity so the grid follows matter (Lagrangian, which distorts under vorticity); or shifts chosen to zero selected components of the 3-metric (isothermal, radial).
concepts.how_introduced: Listed after lapse choices, each with a pro and con.
concepts.notes: Three shift conditions can remove three 3-metric components, e.g. making the spatial line element diagonal (14.124).

concepts.name: gravitational degrees of freedom
concepts.definition: The vacuum gravitational field carries two degrees of freedom per spatial point, corresponding to four freely specifiable initial data (two configuration variables and two velocities) once constraints and all coordinate freedoms are removed.
concepts.how_introduced: Established by an explicit subtraction count within 3+1, then used to criticize 3+1 for not exhibiting these data geometrically.

concepts.name: characteristic initial value problem
concepts.definition: An initial value problem in which data are posed on null hypersurfaces rather than on a spacelike Cauchy surface.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the setting where 3+1 fails and 2+2 excels, with physical motivations (radiation along null directions, null infinity, past light cone in cosmology).

concepts.name: 2+2 formalism
concepts.definition: A covariant splitting of spacetime into a two-parameter family of spacelike 2-surfaces and their orthogonal 2-spaces, using two families of hypersurfaces, projection operators and Lie derivatives along two vector fields.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the two limitations of 3+1, constructed by dragging an initial 2-surface along two transvecting vector fields, attributed to d'Inverno and Smallwood (1980).

concepts.name: double null foliation
concepts.definition: A 2+2 foliation in which both vector fields dragging the initial 2-surface are null, producing two families of null hypersurfaces.
concepts.how_introduced: Illustrated by two ruled sheets emanating from an initial 2-surface (Fig. 14.6).

concepts.name: null-timelike foliation
concepts.definition: A 2+2 foliation with one null and one timelike dragging vector field, producing null cones threaded by a timelike tube.
concepts.how_introduced: Illustrated by nested cones around a central cylinder (Fig. 14.7).

concepts.name: integrable distribution
concepts.definition: A field of 2-planes is tangent to a family of 2-surfaces exactly when the Lie bracket of any two fields spanning it stays in the span; for the dyad here the book uses vanishing bracket as the criterion.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to show the orthogonal 2-spaces {T} are generally not tangent to surfaces, because [n_0, n_1] is generically non-zero.

concepts.name: vector dyad
concepts.definition: A pair of vectors n_A spanning the 2-space orthogonal to the 2-surfaces, dual to the gradients of the two foliation scalars.
concepts.how_introduced: Constructed from the normals to the two hypersurface families.

concepts.name: lapse matrix
concepts.definition: The Gram matrix of the dyad, equal to the dyad components of the metric on the orthogonal 2-space; its diagonal entries play the role of lapses for the two foliations.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined from the dyad and shown to coincide with h_AB, then compared with the scalar lapse of 3+1.

concepts.name: 2+2 shift vectors
concepts.definition: Two vectors tangent to the 2-surfaces that, added to the dyad, give commuting connecting vectors E_A between neighbouring 2-surfaces; they generalize the 3+1 shift.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as the freedom left after fixing duality with the normals; chosen so that [E_0, E_1] = 0 to allow coordinates.

concepts.name: 2+2 decomposition of the metric
concepts.definition: In coordinates with x^0, x^1 given by the two foliation scalars and x^2, x^3 constant along the connecting vectors, the metric has a block form built from the lapse matrix, two shift vectors and the 2-metric of the surfaces.
concepts.how_introduced: Worked out explicitly so it can be compared with the 3+1 block forms.

concepts.name: conformal 2-structure
concepts.definition: The metric of the spacelike 2-surfaces with its overall scale (area element) divided out, leaving two functions that are claimed to carry the two gravitational degrees of freedom.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced at the end of §14.14, with attribution to d'Inverno and Stachel (1978) and the remark that its Euler-Lagrange equations reproduce the two dynamical Einstein equations.

concepts.name: Bondi-type coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates built on outgoing null cones from a timelike geodesic: a retarded time labelling the cones, a radial coordinate along generators, and two angles.
concepts.how_introduced: Only previewed in Fig. 14.9 as an application of 2+2 to be developed in Chapter 23.
