figures.label: Fig. 14.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: A spacelike slice that every causal worldline crosses once.
figures.visual_description: A pale, vertically elongated barrel-shaped region labelled 'Space-time' on the right. A flat grey ellipse cuts horizontally across the middle, labelled 'S spacelike hypersurface' on the left. About six thin roughly vertical curves run bottom to top through the region, each pierced once by the ellipse at a black dot.
figures.what_it_teaches: Definition of a Cauchy surface: every endless causal curve intersects it exactly once, the property underlying global hyperbolicity.

redesign.idea: Cauchy-surface tester: a 2+1 spacetime block with a draggable, deformable slice and a set of random timelike and null worldlines; each crossing lights up, and the slice is flagged as non-Cauchy when any curve crosses twice or misses (e.g. slice tilted to become partly null, or a hole punched in it, or anti-de Sitter-like boundary).
redesign.interaction: Learner sculpts the slice with control points and toggles a removed point in spacetime; crossing counts update per worldline.

figures.label: Fig. 14.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Spacetime sliced into a stack of spacelike leaves.
figures.visual_description: Three separate, gently wavy horizontal ribbons stacked vertically with gaps, labelled Sigma_1 (bottom), Sigma_2 and Sigma_3 (top). No axes, normals or worldlines are drawn.
figures.what_it_teaches: A foliation is an ordered, non-intersecting family of spacelike hypersurfaces filling spacetime.

redesign.idea: Level-set slicer: define a time function t(x, y, T) by a formula or sliders (e.g. flat slices, hyperboloids, boosted slices, maximal-like slices near a mass); render its level sets as a translucent stack with normals drawn, and warn when the gradient stops being timelike (a leaf turns null or timelike).
redesign.interaction: Learner edits the time function and scrubs through t; leaves, normals and a timelike-gradient check update live.

figures.label: Fig. 14.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two neighbouring leaves as seen by a normal observer.
figures.visual_description: Two parallel tilted parallelograms (planes in perspective), one above the other. A point x^a on the lower plane has a small right-angle mark; an arrow rises from it labelled (delta tau) n^a and ends at a point labelled x-tilde^a on the upper plane.
figures.what_it_teaches: Stepping a proper time delta tau along the unit normal lands on the next leaf, which fixes the lapse as proper time per coordinate time.
concepts: unit normal to a spacelike hypersurface

redesign.idea: Lapse clock: two slices t and t + dt with a line of Eulerian observers carrying clocks; a lapse profile N(x) is painted by the learner and the gap between slices stretches locally, while each clock ticks N dt. A companion strip plots A = -grad ln N as arrows along the slice.
redesign.interaction: Learner paints N(x) and steps dt; slice separations, clock readings and acceleration arrows update.

figures.label: Fig. 14.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Threading curves and the split of the evolution vector into lapse and shift parts.
figures.visual_description: Two wavy near-horizontal curves: Sigma_t (lower) and Sigma_{t+dt} (upper). Two dashed curves rising slightly to the right cross both, labelled x^alpha and x^alpha + dx^alpha at the bottom. From a point on the lower slice a vertical arrow labelled n^a N dt meets the upper slice; a slanted arrow labelled T^a dt goes from the same point along the dashed thread; a short horizontal arrow labelled beta^a dt on the upper slice closes the triangle, and a segment dx^alpha is marked along the upper slice between the threads.
figures.what_it_teaches: The evolution vector is the normal step (lapse) plus a sideways step within the slice (shift); coordinates stay constant along the threads, which is what makes the metric pick up g_{0 mu} terms.

redesign.idea: Lapse-shift triangle builder: in 1+1 or 2+1 Minkowski or Schwarzschild space, pick a slicing and drag the threading curves; the triangle N n dt + beta dt = T dt is drawn at each grid point and the resulting line element coefficients g_00 = N^2 - beta.beta, g_0x = -beta_x, g_xx are shown numerically, with a check that the proper interval along T matches.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags lapse and shift handles at grid points (or chooses presets: zero shift, rotating grid, Painleve-Gullstrand); metric components and grid distortion update.

figures.label: Fig. 14.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: An initial 2-surface and two vector fields leaving it.
figures.visual_description: A single large parallelogram in perspective labelled S_0 near its lower right edge. From the midpoint of the top far edge two arrows point out of the surface in different directions, labelled v_1 and v_2.
figures.what_it_teaches: The 2+2 construction starts from a spacelike 2-surface and two independent vector fields not tangent to it. (The text calls the fields n_0 and n_1; the figure labels them v_1 and v_2.)

redesign.idea: Surface dragger: a 2-surface patch in a 3D projection of spacetime with two draggable direction handles at each point; flowing along each field sweeps out a 3-surface, colour-coded by causal character (null, timelike, spacelike) of its generator.
redesign.interaction: Learner rotates the two direction handles and presses flow; the two swept families of 3-surfaces appear with causal labels.

figures.label: Fig. 14.6
figures.visual_description: Two ruled planar sheets meeting along a common edge in a V or open-book shape; each sheet is hatched with parallel slanted lines (generators). Near the crease a label reads 'S_0: initial 2-surface', with short arrows v_1 and v_2 pointing along each sheet.
figures.what_it_teaches: Dragging the initial 2-surface along two null fields produces two intersecting families of null hypersurfaces.

redesign.idea: Double-null book: in 1+1 Minkowski (plus suppressed sphere) show u = t - r and v = t + r level lines as a lattice of light rays; select a grid cell to see its 2-sphere and the two null normals; switch to a Schwarzschild or colliding-wave background where the lattice distorts.
redesign.interaction: Learner scrubs u and v independently, watching the 2-surface S(u, v) move along each null direction.

figures.label: Fig. 14.7
figures.visual_description: A cone that opens upward like a funnel, drawn with horizontal rings, with a narrow ringed vertical cylinder rising along its axis and continuing above the rim. Dashed vertical lines inside mark the part of the cylinder hidden by the cone. A small ring at the narrow lower end is labelled 'S_0: initial 2-surface'. From a point on it, an arrow v_1 points out along the cone surface and an arrow v_2 points straight up.
figures.what_it_teaches: One null field sweeps out a light cone and one timelike field sweeps out a timelike world tube; together they foliate spacetime, the geometry of radiation problems with a central source.

redesign.idea: World-tube and cones: a source's worldtube emits nested outgoing null cones; the learner moves along the tube (retarded time u) and along cone generators (r), with the current 2-sphere highlighted and its area shown, previewing Bondi coordinates in Chapter 23.
redesign.interaction: Learner scrubs u and r; the highlighted sphere and the ring of null generators move accordingly.

figures.label: Fig. 14.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: The 2-space orthogonal to the 2-surface at a point.
figures.visual_description: A horizontal parallelogram labelled S and an upright rectangle labelled T intersecting through a common point P marked with a dot; the part of S behind T is dashed.
figures.what_it_teaches: At each point the tangent space splits into the 2-plane tangent to the spacelike 2-surface and the orthogonal timelike 2-plane spanned by the dyad; the orthogonal planes need not mesh into surfaces.

redesign.idea: Integrability checker: a grid of little orthogonal planes {T} attached to points of a 2+2 slicing; the learner tries to 'stitch' them into surfaces, and the tool shows the closure failure of a small dyad loop proportional to [n_0, n_1], vanishing when the configuration is holonomic.
redesign.interaction: Learner adjusts a twist parameter in the foliation functions and traces loops; the gap vector and bracket magnitude update.

figures.label: Fig. 14.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: Coordinates built from null cones along a timelike geodesic.
figures.visual_description: A slanted straight line labelled 'Timelike geodesic' rising through two upward-opening cones. The lower cone, with apex on the line, is labelled u = u_0 and 'N_0: initial null cone'; an arrow labelled r runs outward along it. The upper cone is labelled u = u_1. A curved arrow at the bottom is labelled theta, phi, indicating the angular coordinates.
figures.what_it_teaches: Bondi-type coordinates: retarded time labels future null cones from a central geodesic, r runs along generators, and angles label generators; initial data are posed on a null cone.

redesign.idea: Cone-coordinate explorer: pick an event and read off (u, r, theta, phi) by finding which cone from the worldline passes through it; show how an outgoing wave packet stays at nearly fixed u as r grows, contrasting with its changing t on 3+1 slices.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags an event or launches a pulse; coordinate readouts and cone highlighting update.

worked_examples.problem: Show that B applied to any vector gives a vector orthogonal to n, and that B is a projector.
worked_examples.method: Contract B_b^a X^b with n_a and use n.n = 1; for idempotence multiply two copies of delta - n n.
worked_examples.key_insight: Both properties reduce to the single fact B n = 0, which in turn is just the normalization of n.
concepts: unit normal to a spacelike hypersurface

worked_examples.problem: Show that the induced derivative D annihilates the induced metric and hence is the Levi-Civita derivative of h.
worked_examples.method: Write h = g - n n inside the projected derivative, drop nabla g, expand nabla(n n) by Leibniz, and note each term leaves a bare n contracted with a projector.
worked_examples.key_insight: Projection kills anything carrying a free normal index, so metric compatibility is inherited; torsion-freeness (Exercise 14.3) then gives uniqueness.
worked_examples.result: D_e h_ab = 0; D is the metric derivative of h (and of gamma).

worked_examples.problem: Relate the 4D and 3D Christoffel symbols in adapted coordinates and split the tangential derivative into tangent and normal parts.
worked_examples.method: Compare the coordinate form of D X in terms of 4D Gamma with its form as the 3-metric derivative; for the normal part, differentiate n.X = 0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Tangential projection of nabla sees only intrinsic geometry; the leftover normal part is exactly K(X, Y), yielding the Gauss formula.
worked_examples.result: Gamma^beta_{alpha gamma} *= (3)Gamma^beta_{alpha gamma}; nabla_Y X = D_Y X + K(X,Y) n.

worked_examples.problem: Express the normal-normal and normal-tangential components of the Einstein tensor in terms of slice data.
worked_examples.method: Contract the Gauss equation with g^{ac} = h^{ac} + n^a n^c, contract again, and compare with G_ab n^a n^b = R_ab n n - R/2; contract Codazzi once and note the g_cd R term dies under B n.
worked_examples.key_insight: The four components of G with at least one normal index contain no second normal derivatives, so they are constraints rather than evolution equations.

worked_examples.method: Expand D_a D_b Z^c with projectors, differentiate the projectors using (14.37), evaluate the two projector-derivative terms as n K, use n.Z = 0 to get Z K, antisymmetrize, then strip an arbitrary vector.
worked_examples.key_insight: All the extrinsic information enters through derivatives of the projectors; antisymmetrization removes the term proportional to K_ab n^d.
worked_examples.result: (3)R_abcd = BBBB R_efgh + K_ac K_bd - K_ad K_bc.

worked_examples.method: Apply the projected derivative to K = -B B nabla n, expand the projectors by Leibniz, cancel symmetric terms under a<->c, and convert the commutator of nabla on n into Riemann.
worked_examples.key_insight: The normal index of the resulting Riemann component comes from the covector being differentiated.
worked_examples.result: D_a K_bc - D_c K_ba = -B B B R^l_{kgj} n_l.

worked_examples.problem: Derive the Ricci equation for the normal-normal curvature component.
worked_examples.method: Decompose nabla n = -K + n A, substitute in the Lie-derivative formula for L_n K, rewrite n.nabla K through second derivatives of n, split nabla A into D A plus normal pieces, and replace the commutator on n by Riemann.
worked_examples.key_insight: Only with a foliation can n be differentiated along itself; the acceleration is exactly the extra datum that closes the curvature reconstruction.
worked_examples.result: L_n K_ab = n n R_dbca + A_a A_b - D_a A_b - K_a^c K_cb.
concepts: decomposition of the gradient of the normal

worked_examples.problem: Show that the lapse equals proper time per coordinate time for Eulerian observers.
worked_examples.method: Move from event x by delta tau along n; Taylor expand t to first order; use n^b partial_b t = w_b n^b = 1/N.
worked_examples.key_insight: The gradient of t contracted with the unit normal counts how many coordinate-time units one proper-time unit covers.
worked_examples.result: delta t = delta tau / N, so N = d tau / dt.

worked_examples.problem: Show that the extrinsic curvature is minus half the normal Lie derivative of the induced metric.
worked_examples.method: Write h = g - n n; L_n g = nabla_a n_b + nabla_b n_a; L_n(n n) = A n + n A (Exercise 14.8); substitute the gradient decomposition.
worked_examples.key_insight: The acceleration pieces cancel against those in nabla n, leaving only K: the extrinsic curvature is the 'velocity' of the 3-metric.
worked_examples.result: L_n h_ab = -2 K_ab; in Eulerian coordinates gamma-dot = 2 N K.
concepts: extrinsic curvature as rate of change of the induced metric

worked_examples.problem: Remove the acceleration from the Ricci equation using the lapse.
worked_examples.method: Use A = -D ln N to show D_a A_b - A_a A_b = -(1/N) D_a D_b N (the (DN)(DN)/N^2 terms cancel), then substitute and use the contracted Gauss equation.
worked_examples.key_insight: Everything about how slices are spaced is encoded in the Hessian of the lapse divided by the lapse.
worked_examples.result: Evolution equation (14.77) for K along n.
concepts: evolution equation for the extrinsic curvature

worked_examples.problem: Construct the 3+1 metric from lapse, shift and 3-metric.
worked_examples.method: Split T = N n + beta, solve for n, substitute into g^{ab} = h^{ab} + n^a n^b, evaluate in coordinates with T = partial_t, compute the determinant relation, and invert blockwise.
worked_examples.key_insight: The coordinate threads determine g_{0 mu}: zero shift gives a block-diagonal metric; the spatial block of the inverse metric equals -gamma^{mu nu} only for zero shift.
worked_examples.result: g^{ab} and g_ab block forms and the line element (14.90) (with sign corrections noted under key_equations).

worked_examples.problem: Convert the geometric evolution equations into coordinate PDEs for gamma and K.
worked_examples.method: Split L_T = L_{Nn} + L_beta; show the gradient-of-N terms vanish because they contract n with tangential tensors; expand L_beta with D because beta is tangent; evaluate in adapted coordinates.
worked_examples.key_insight: Lie derivatives along the coordinate time vector are just partial_t, so the geometric statements become an explicit first-order system; lapse and shift appear only as given coefficients.

worked_examples.problem: Construct constraint-satisfying initial data with the simplest conformal choices.
worked_examples.method: Take conformally flat Cartesian gamma-hat, maximal K = 0 and zero free TT data T-hat; substitute into the conformal Hamiltonian and momentum constraints.
worked_examples.key_insight: The momentum constraint becomes a linear, decoupled vector Laplace equation for X, after which the Hamiltonian constraint is a single nonlinear scalar equation for psi; analytic momentum solutions exist for boosted and spinning black holes.
worked_examples.result: Delta-hat psi = -(1/8)(ell X)^2 psi^-7 (book prints -18) and Delta_ell X = 0.

worked_examples.problem: Count the true gravitational degrees of freedom.
worked_examples.method: Start with 10 metric functions; remove 4 coordinate choices (6 left); initial data are gamma and K (12) minus 4 constraints (8); remove 3 spatial coordinate choices on the slice (5); remove 1 embedding (slicing) condition such as K = 0 (4); interpret as 2 q plus 2 q-dot.
worked_examples.key_insight: Every gauge freedom removes data twice (once as a choice, once via the constraint it generates), so 10 components leave only 2 dynamical degrees of freedom.
worked_examples.result: Two degrees of freedom; the 3+1 formalism nonetheless carries six evolution equations and does not exhibit which data are free.

worked_examples.method: Define the dual dyad, the Gram matrix N_AB, projectors onto the 2-surfaces and orthogonal spaces, connecting vectors E_A with commuting shifts b_A, and adapted coordinates; read off contravariant components and verify the covariant form by block multiplication (Exercise 14.12).
worked_examples.key_insight: The single lapse becomes a 2x2 lapse matrix and the single shift becomes two shift vectors, but the structure of the block matrices mirrors 3+1.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A slice of spacetime as an 'instant of time' and spacetime as the time history of a 3-geometry (geometrodynamics)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Recasts Einstein's static 4D equations as ordinary-looking dynamics: the configuration is the 3-metric, its velocity is (essentially) the extrinsic curvature, and the field equations push the pair forward in t.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Which slices count as 'instants' is a free choice (the lapse and shift), so there is no preferred universal time; different slicings of the same spacetime give different-looking histories.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Film-strip view: a 3-geometry rendered as an embedded surface frame by frame, with a toggle that re-slices the same spacetime and shows a different film of the same 4-geometry.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The unit normal as the 4-velocity of an observer, its acceleration as that observer's felt acceleration, and the lapse as that observer's clock rate
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives physical meaning to n^a, A^a = n.nabla n and N: slices are the observer's simultaneity surfaces, and N converts coordinate time into proper time.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Eulerian observers are a mathematical congruence, not the grid of the actual coordinates when the shift is non-zero; they may not correspond to any physically preferred matter.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Clock-carrying observers on a slicing with a painted lapse; tick counters and acceleration arrows update.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Lagrangian mechanics bookkeeping: two coordinates q and two velocities q-dot
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The four freely specifiable data left after the count are read as two configuration pieces (in the metric) and two velocity pieces (in the extrinsic curvature), i.e. two degrees of freedom.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The count is per spatial point in a field theory; which components are the q's is not identified by 3+1 (the complaint that motivates 2+2).
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Subtraction ladder animation from 10 down to 2 with each removal labelled by its reason.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Eulerian versus Lagrangian descriptions of fluid flow
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Implicit in the naming: Eulerian gauge (zero shift) keeps the grid normal to slices like a fixed laboratory mesh, while Lagrangian slicing and gauge move the coordinates with the matter, like following fluid parcels.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: In GR the 'fixed mesh' still moves in spacetime along the normal and is not attached to any background; and grid tangling under vorticity is a practical, not conceptual, failure.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side grids in a rotating fluid flow: Eulerian grid stays regular, Lagrangian grid twists and tangles over time.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Projection of vectors onto a plane, as in taking the shadow of an arrow
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: B = delta - n n behaves like removing the component along a unit normal; the book stresses idempotence 'as one would expect from a projection operator'.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: With a timelike normal in Lorentzian signature the 'orthogonal complement' is defined by the spacetime metric, not by Euclidean perpendicularity, so pictures drawn on paper mislead about angles.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Minkowski-diagram projector: drag a vector and a tilted slice; the projected part and removed normal part are drawn with Lorentzian orthogonality shown correctly.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The origin of 'globally hyperbolic' in the hyperbolic wave equation
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The name is explained by the existence of unique global solutions to the wave equation, linking a causal-structure definition to familiar PDE behaviour.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The name refers to a property of spacetime, not to any hyperbolic geometry of the slices.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Promoting the scalar lapse to a 2x2 matrix and the single shift to a pair of shifts
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The authors explicitly ask the reader to compare the 2+2 block metrics with the 3+1 ones, so familiar 3+1 roles transfer to the new objects.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: In the null cases the lapse matrix has zero diagonal entries, so its 'lapse' interpretation as a proper-time rate breaks down.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toggle between 3+1 and 2+2 block matrices with matching colours for lapse, shift and spatial metric blocks.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The extrinsic curvature is defined as minus half the time derivative (Lie derivative along n) of the spatial metric.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: That identity holds only when a foliation exists; the primary definition uses the tangential derivative of the normal and makes sense for a single hypersurface.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Numerical-relativity treatments often start from the Lie-derivative formula because they always have a foliation.
concepts: extrinsic curvature as rate of change of the induced metric

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The spatial part of the inverse spacetime metric equals minus the inverse spatial metric.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: g^{alpha beta} = -gamma^{alpha beta} + beta^alpha beta^beta / N^2, so the equality holds only when the shift vanishes (while g_{alpha beta} = -gamma_{alpha beta} always holds in adapted coordinates).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The covariant spatial block does equal -gamma, so learners assume inverting blocks commutes.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Lapse and shift are physical fields that must be evolved along with the metric.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Einstein's equations give no evolution equations for them; they are gauge functions chosen freely (or by imposed conditions) to fix coordinates.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: They appear in every equation and in the metric, alongside dynamical variables.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Knowing the induced metric and extrinsic curvature of one slice determines the full spacetime curvature there.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Gauss and Codazzi fix every component except the normal-normal ones R_{alpha 0 beta 0}, which need derivatives of the normal off the slice (the Ricci equation, requiring a foliation).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter opens by saying (gamma, K) are the key data, and they do suffice as initial data once the field equations are imposed.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Ten metric components with ten field equations means ten independent gravitational degrees of freedom.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Coordinate freedom, constraints and slicing freedom reduce this to four free data, i.e. two degrees of freedom per point.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Counting unknowns and equations works in simpler field theories without gauge symmetry.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Sign differences between this chapter and numerical-relativity papers mean one of them is wrong.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Most differences come from the (+,-,-,-) versus (-,+,+,+) signature, which flips the orientation convention for the normal (n = N grad t versus n = -N grad t) and the sign of K; always translate conventions before comparing.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The equations look almost identical apart from signs.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The 2-planes orthogonal to a family of 2-surfaces automatically mesh together into orthogonal 2-surfaces.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They do so only if the dyad spanning them has vanishing (or in-span) Lie bracket; generically they are not integrable.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In 3+1, the orthogonal complement is one-dimensional and always integrates to curves, and in flat-space pictures orthogonal planes look like they stack.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If spacetime is flat the slices must have zero curvature, and a curved slice means a curved spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Intrinsic curvature of a slice and extrinsic curvature both depend on how it is embedded: hyperboloidal slices of Minkowski space have negative intrinsic curvature balanced by non-zero K in the Gauss equation, while flat slices of curved spacetimes exist (e.g. Painleve-Gullstrand slices of Schwarzschild).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Learners conflate the curvature of the 4-geometry with that of the 3-geometry of a slice.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Once constraints hold initially, a numerical evolution will keep them satisfied automatically.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The Bianchi identities preserve them for exact solutions of the evolution equations; numerically, truncation errors excite constraint violations that can grow, which is why constraint monitoring and damping formulations are used.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book states the exact preservation result without numerical caveats.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A foliation reveals the physically true simultaneity of spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The leaves are simultaneous only for the Eulerian observers of that chosen slicing; a different time function gives different leaves for the same spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The 'instant of time' language and the stacked-sheet picture suggest a universal present.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Singularity-avoiding slicings remove singularities from the spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They only slow the evolution of slices near the singularity (lapse collapsing toward zero) so the computational slices never reach it; the spacetime is unchanged.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The phrase 'avoidance' sounds like a physical effect.

thought_experiments.name: A small proper-time step along the normal
thought_experiments.setup: An Eulerian observer at an event on one leaf waits a short proper time and asks which leaf they are now on.
thought_experiments.lesson: The coordinate-time label advances by the proper time divided by N, so the lapse is the ratio of elapsed proper time to elapsed coordinate time.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Two adjustable slices with an observer clock; varying N changes the proper time ticks needed to reach the next slice.

thought_experiments.name: Endless worldlines crossing a candidate initial surface
thought_experiments.setup: Draw every endless timelike and null curve through a region and count how many times each crosses a proposed spacelike slice.
thought_experiments.lesson: Only if every curve crosses exactly once does the slice qualify as a Cauchy surface capable of determining the whole spacetime.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Crossing counter overlay on a user-deformable slice.

thought_experiments.name: Dragging a 2-surface along two vector fields
thought_experiments.setup: Choose a spacelike 2-surface in a bare manifold and two vector fields crossing it; flow the surface along each field.
thought_experiments.lesson: The flows generate two foliations of 3-surfaces whose causal character (double null, null-timelike) is set by the chosen vector fields, which is the constructive starting point of 2+2.
thought_experiments.app_idea: 3D flow tool sweeping sheets from an initial patch with causal colour coding.

thought_experiments.name: Freely falling slicing during collapse
thought_experiments.setup: Evolve a collapsing star with unit lapse and zero shift, so coordinate observers fall freely, versus maximal slicing.
thought_experiments.lesson: Freely falling (and comoving) observers converge on the singularity so the slicing crashes into it; keeping K = 0 prevents focusing and holds the slices back.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Oppenheimer-Snyder style collapse diagram with slices drawn for geodesic versus maximal slicing, showing the lapse collapsing in the latter.

thought_experiments.name: Coordinates riding on a swirling fluid
thought_experiments.setup: Set the shift equal to the fluid 3-velocity in a two- or three-dimensional flow with vorticity.
thought_experiments.lesson: The grid follows the matter and becomes severely twisted, destroying numerical accuracy; comoving coordinates work well only in one-dimensional flows.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Grid advected by a vortex flow with a distortion meter.

historical_notes.event: Wrote Einstein's equations as a constraint-plus-evolution system on hypersurfaces in the special case of unit lapse and zero shift (Gaussian normal coordinates).
historical_notes.significance: First geometric initial value formulation; also gave an analytic existence argument.

historical_notes.event: Extended the formulation to a general lapse with zero shift; his lemma on constraint preservation is invoked in the degree-of-freedom count.
historical_notes.significance: Generalized slicing and established that constraints propagate via the Bianchi identities.

historical_notes.significance: Completed the geometric 3+1 system; her later work underpins well-posedness for non-analytic data.

historical_notes.event: Derived a Hamiltonian formulation of GR with the metric and a momentum built from the extrinsic curvature as canonical variables.
historical_notes.significance: Source of the names 'Hamiltonian constraint', 'momentum constraint' and 'ADM formalism'.

historical_notes.event: Coined 'geometrodynamics' for GR viewed as evolving 3-geometry.
historical_notes.significance: Frames the conceptual picture of the chapter.

historical_notes.event: Developed the conformal approach that turns the constraints into elliptic equations for a conformal factor and vector potential.
historical_notes.significance: Standard method for constructing initial data in numerical relativity.

applications_and_observations.topic: Numerical relativity of gravitational collapse and gravitational waves
applications_and_observations.details: The 3+1 equations are the framework for computer solutions of Einstein's equations and underpin the modern understanding of collapse and gravitational radiation. (Tutor context, not in the book: the long-standing binary black hole problem was solved in 2005 by Pretorius and by the Campanelli et al. and Baker et al. groups, and such simulations inform waveform models used in LIGO-Virgo detections starting with GW150914 in 2015; production codes use BSSN or generalized-harmonic reformulations rather than raw ADM.)
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our additions: first full binary black hole merger simulations 2005; first detection 14 September 2015.

applications_and_observations.topic: Analytic initial data for black holes with chosen momentum and spin
applications_and_observations.details: With a conformally flat metric, maximal slicing and no free TT data, the momentum constraint is linear and decoupled and can be solved analytically for one or more black holes with specified linear and angular momenta; the Hamiltonian constraint is then solved for the conformal factor. (The book does not name them; these are the Bowen-York solutions.)
Used the Eulerian gauge (zero shift), with coordinate lines normal to the slices.

applications_and_observations.topic: Radial gauge for radiation in asymptotically flat spacetimes
applications_and_observations.details: Shift chosen to set gamma_{r theta} = gamma_{r phi} = 0 and fix the angular determinant to r^4 sin^2 theta, giving a three-function spatial metric suited to extracting gravitational radiation.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Three metric functions A, B, xi.

applications_and_observations.topic: Characteristic evolution for radiation, null infinity and cosmology
applications_and_observations.details: Null initial value problems are natural because gravitational radiation travels along null geodesics, null infinity is a null hypersurface (so it can be included in the computational domain and radiation defined unambiguously), and cosmological information arrives along our past light cone.
Subtraction chain from metric components to dynamical degrees of freedom in vacuum.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 10 components -> 6 after 4 coordinate choices; 12 initial data (gamma, K) -> 8 after 4 constraints -> 5 after 3 spatial coordinate choices -> 4 after 1 slicing condition = 2 q + 2 q-dot -> 2 degrees of freedom.

notation_and_conventions.convention: (+,-,-,-); the future-pointing unit normal satisfies n_a n^a = +1; the induced metric h_ab is negative definite on the slice.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Numerical-relativity literature uses (-,+,+,+), where the future-pointing normal is n^a = -N grad^a t and many signs (K, constraint terms) differ; the book warns about this twice.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Positive definite spatial metric used for ADM variables; in §14.10 Greek indices are raised and lowered with gamma.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Many printed equations (constraints, K evolution) have signs appropriate to contractions with h; see gaps.

notation_and_conventions.convention: An equality valid only in a particular (adapted) coordinate system.
Latin a, b, ... = 0-3 spacetime; Greek alpha, beta, mu, nu = 1-3 on the slice; in 2+2, bold A, B = 0, 1 label the two foliations/dyad and i, j = 2, 3 label coordinates on the 2-surfaces.
K is minus the projected gradient of the future-pointing normal, equivalently minus half the normal Lie derivative of h; with zero shift the coordinate-time derivative of gamma is 2NK.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Opposite in sign to the common (-,+,+,+) convention K_ij = -(1/2) L_n gamma_ij.

notation_and_conventions.convention: [D_a, D_b] Z^c = (3)R^c_{dab} Z^d, the same convention as the 4D tensor in earlier chapters.
(3)R, (3)R_ab, (3)Gamma denote objects built from the 3-metric; ^2g_ij the 2-metric of the 2+2 surfaces and ^2g-bar_ij its conformal structure; hats denote conformal background quantities.
Lapse N (also written alpha in §14.10-14.12); shift beta^a; rigging vector T^a = N n^a + beta^a; 2+2 lapse matrix N_AB and shifts b_A^a with connecting vectors E_A.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The switch between N and alpha is unannounced.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Written L with a bold vector subscript (L_n, L_T, L_beta, L_{Nn}).

A^a is the acceleration but A^{mu nu} is the trace-free extrinsic curvature; T^a is the rigging vector, T_b^a the 2+2 projector and T-hat^{mu nu} the free TT data; gamma is the 3-metric and, in §14.14, the determinant of the 2-metric; h_ab is the induced 3-metric and, in §14.14, the metric on the orthogonal 2-space; B_a^b projects onto the 3-slice and, in §14.14, onto the 2-surface.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Flag these for learners moving between sections.

margin_notes.summary: Christoffel symbols of h and of gamma = -h coincide, because they are unchanged when the metric changes overall sign.
Numerical relativists using (-,+,+,+) take n = -N grad t to keep the lapse positive, so their equations differ in sign.
Defining K through the Lie derivative of the metric presupposes a foliation, whereas the tangential-derivative definition needs only one surface.
The spatial inverse-metric block equals -gamma^{alpha beta} only in zero-shift coordinates.
Lapse and shift carry the same information as g_{0a}, the part of the data that had to be specified in Chapter 13.
Section 14.12 departs from the book's habit and mostly quotes literature results without derivation.
The 2+2 formalism is only outlined because it looks complicated, but it rests on the same projection and Lie-derivative tools; only the metric decomposition is done in detail.
Bondi's radiating metric, an application of the 2+2 approach, and null hypersurfaces in gravitational radiation are deferred to Chapter 23.
Further reading notes that many numerical-relativity treatments jump straight to lapse and shift and use the opposite signature.

notable.summary: Three parts: tangent fields have tangent brackets; the antisymmetrized induced derivatives equal the projection of the spacetime ones; conclude the tangential and spacetime expressions agree and hence the induced derivative has no torsion.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the missing half of the proof that D is the Levi-Civita derivative of h. Part (ii) prints a lowered index X_b that should be raised.

notable.summary: For the t = 0 slice of the general time-dependent spherically symmetric metric with functions nu(t, r) and lambda(t, r), find the positive definite 3-metric and extrinsic curvature.
notable.why_notable: The only concrete, component-level calculation in the chapter; it previews §15.4 and shows K is controlled by the time derivative of lambda.

notable.summary: Show that the Gauss and Codazzi equations give all spacetime curvature components in terms of gamma and K except R_{alpha 0 beta 0}, using the unit normal for the same metric.
notable.why_notable: Makes the 'all but one projection' claim concrete. The hint writes the normal with upper index as (e^{nu/2}, 0, 0, 0), which is the covector n_a; the vector is n^a = (e^{-nu/2}, 0, 0, 0).

notable.summary: Split the gradient of the normal into extrinsic curvature and acceleration pieces by inserting the projector on each index, then derive the formula for the normal derivative of K used in the Ricci equation.
notable.why_notable: The single most reused identity of the chapter.

notable.summary: Using n = (1/N) partial_t in coordinates carried by normal observers, rewrite K = -(1/2) L_n h as gamma-dot = 2NK.
notable.why_notable: Connects the abstract K to the time derivative that numerical codes evolve.

notable.summary: Show that the acceleration of normal observers is minus the spatial gradient of the logarithm of the lapse.
notable.why_notable: Physically striking: gravity-like acceleration of hovering observers is encoded in how the lapse varies across a slice (compare the Newtonian limit N ~ 1 + Phi).

notable.summary: Four parts: express the 2-metric via the lapse matrix, write the dyad through connecting vectors and shifts, use adapted coordinates to build the 2+2 contravariant metric, and confirm the covariant form by block multiplication.
notable.why_notable: The only hands-on 2+2 exercise; it checks the comparison with 3+1 and exposes the structure of the lapse matrix.

difficulty.notes: Among the most technical chapters of the book: long projector-laden index derivations (Gauss, Codazzi, Ricci), Lie derivatives, and block-matrix inversion, with many steps delegated to exercises. Conceptually the layering (slice, foliation, fibration) is clear, but distinguishing intrinsic from extrinsic geometry, gauge from dynamics, and h from gamma sign conventions is demanding. §14.12 and §14.13-14.14 shift to quoted results with little derivation. Several misprints and sign inconsistencies (14.76, 14.87, 14.89-90, 14.121, 14.123, 14.142, the h/gamma remark) will derail careful learners who try to verify equations.

teaching_gems.gem: Build the geometry in three layers: one slice (h, K), then a stack of slices (acceleration, lapse, Ricci equation), then threads through the stack (shift, coordinates), each layer adding exactly the object the previous one could not supply.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners see why lapse and shift exist instead of meeting them as unexplained metric functions, and can locate every quantity by the minimal structure it needs.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Three-stage builder: stage 1 shows a single draggable slice with normals and K; stage 2 unlocks a stack and clocks; stage 3 unlocks threading curves and shows the resulting line element.

teaching_gems.gem: Read K as the part of the spacetime derivative of a tangent vector that sticks out of the slice: nabla_Y X = D_Y X + K(X, Y) n.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns an abstract definition with projectors into a picture familiar from curves and surfaces in 3D: moving along a curved surface, the velocity changes partly out of the surface.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Drag a tangent vector along a curve on an embedded surface (Euclidean then Minkowski); decompose its rate of change into tangential and normal arrows with the normal length equal to K(X, X).

teaching_gems.gem: Curvature reconstruction scorecard: Gauss gives the all-tangential Riemann components, Codazzi those with one normal index, and Ricci those with two; only the last needs more than a single slice.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Organizes three intimidating equations as a complete partition of Riemann by number of normal indices, which also explains why constraints come from the first two.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Interactive Riemann component table (in adapted coordinates) coloured by which equation determines each entry; hovering an entry shows the relevant formula.

teaching_gems.gem: Constraints are exactly the Einstein components with a normal index, and they contain only slice data and tangential derivatives, so they restrict data instead of evolving it.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Connects the abstract counting of constraints with an operational test: look for second time derivatives.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Equation highlighter that colours time-derivative terms in each projection of G_ab, showing which have none.

teaching_gems.gem: The lapse as proper time per coordinate time, derived by stepping delta tau along the normal and Taylor expanding the time function.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A two-line calculation gives a clock-rate meaning that transfers directly to g_00 and to the Newtonian limit.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Lapse clock widget: paint N(x) and watch Eulerian clocks tick at different rates between the same pair of slices.

teaching_gems.gem: The lapse-shift triangle: coordinate evolution vector T dt = normal step N n dt + sideways slide beta dt, from which the metric follows by g^{ab} = h^{ab} + n n.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A single vector diagram generates the entire 3+1 line element, including why a shift produces dt dx cross terms.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Triangle builder in Minkowski or Schwarzschild coordinates showing live metric coefficients as learners drag N and beta.

teaching_gems.gem: Degree-of-freedom subtraction ladder from 10 to 2, used to motivate a better formalism.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives a memorable numeric storyline and a question (which are the two?) that 3+1 cannot answer.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Animated ladder where each rung removes coloured blocks labelled 'coordinate choice', 'constraint', 'slice coordinates', 'slicing condition'.

teaching_gems.gem: Present the 2+2 metric as block matrices directly comparable to the 3+1 ones: the scalar lapse becomes a 2x2 lapse matrix and the shift becomes two shifts.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Leverages hard-won 3+1 understanding to make a less familiar formalism readable at a glance.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Side-by-side colour-coded matrices with a slider morphing 3+1 into 2+2 by splitting one time direction into two.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The note after (14.31) claims the Hamiltonian constraint is unchanged if gamma = -h is used for the contractions. This holds for K^2 and K_ab K^ab but not for (3)R: the Ricci tensor is invariant under h -> -h while the scalar (3)R = h^{ab}R_ab flips sign. Consequently (14.93), which says (3)R is that of gamma with gamma raising, has the wrong sign of (3)R relative to (14.30).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A careful learner checking a known case (e.g. hyperboloidal slices of Minkowski space, or a comparison with numerical-relativity texts) will find the constraint fails and lose trust in the derivation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Teach one convention: with gamma and its scalar curvature, the vacuum Hamiltonian constraint is (3)R + K^2 - K_ab K^ab = 0 (K sign irrelevant here). Verify with the hyperboloid slice t^2 - r^2 = tau^2: (3)R = -6/tau^2, K_ab = gamma_ab/tau up to sign.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Metric block misprints: in (14.87) the off-diagonal inverse-metric entry is printed -beta^mu/N but substitution into (14.82) gives -beta^mu/N^2; in (14.89)-(14.90) g_00 is printed N^2 + beta^sigma beta_sigma, but g(T, T) = N^2 + h_{mu nu} beta^mu beta^nu = N^2 - beta^sigma beta_sigma with gamma lowering, and only that sign inverts (14.87).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Block multiplication checks fail; learners may think the shift contributes positively to g_00, contrary to e.g. the Painleve-Gullstrand or rotating-frame metrics.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use g^{0 mu} = -beta^mu/N^2 and ds^2 = (N^2 - beta_sigma beta^sigma) dt^2 - 2 beta_mu dt dx^mu - gamma_{mu nu} dx^mu dx^nu; verify on flat space in rotating coordinates.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: (14.76) contains an extra -2K_ac K_b^c term that does not follow from (14.61) and the preceding simplification; (14.77), where the -2KK term legitimately appears after using the contracted Gauss equation, is correct.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Exercise 14.11 (derive 14.77 from 14.76 and 14.27) cannot be done consistently from the printed 14.76.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: As the intermediate step, keep only three terms on the right: the doubly normal-contracted Riemann tensor, a single K-squared product, and the lapse Hessian divided by the lapse (see the corrected (14.76) under key_equations).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Shift-term and K-quadratic signs in (14.102), (14.103) and (14.107) are those obtained when indices are moved with h, although §14.10 says Greek indices are moved with gamma. With gamma lowering, (14.102) should read partial_t gamma = 2NK + D beta + D beta and the K K terms in (14.107) change sign.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Implementing the equations in code, or comparing with Gourgoulhon or Baumgarte-Shapiro, produces sign mismatches that look like errors.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the convention explicitly in the app; preferably present the evolution system in the (-,+,+,+) numerical-relativity form alongside a conversion table (K_book = -K_NR, traces with gamma).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: (14.121) prints the coefficient -18; setting R-hat = K = T-hat = 0 in (14.117) gives -1/8 (a lost fraction bar).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Wrong factor of 144 if used to build black-hole initial data.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use Delta-hat psi = -(1/8)(ell-hat X)^{mu nu}(ell-hat X)_{mu nu} psi^{-7}.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The maximal-slicing lapse equation (14.123) introduces matter terms rho and S that are never defined in this vacuum-only chapter and appears to lack a factor of the lapse on the right-hand side; no derivation is given.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners cannot reproduce or use the equation, and may not realise it is linear homogeneous in the lapse in vacuum.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Derive it: set K = 0 and partial_t K = 0 in the trace of the K evolution equation and use the Hamiltonian constraint; in vacuum it reduces to a homogeneous elliptic equation D^2 N = N K_ab K^ab (sign per convention).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: (14.142) prints the conformal 2-structure as gamma^{-2} times the 2-metric with gamma its determinant, which is not scale-free; a unit-determinant structure requires the power -1/2. The same section also calls (14.139) the 'contravariant' metric and reuses gamma and h for new objects.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The central claim that the conformal structure carries two functions (a symmetric 2x2 matrix with fixed determinant) becomes opaque.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write ^2g-bar_ij = |^2g|^{-1/2} ^2g_ij and count: 3 components minus 1 scale = 2.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Symmetry of K (14.20) is asserted in one line from torsion-freeness; for a single hypersurface the argument really uses that the Lie bracket of tangent fields is tangent, which is only proved later as Exercise 14.3(i).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think symmetry holds for the projected gradient of any unit timelike field, which is false for twisting congruences.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show K(X,Y) - K(Y,X) = n.[X,Y] (up to sign) and note it vanishes because the bracket is tangent; contrast with a rotating congruence where it does not.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The product-topology result for globally hyperbolic spacetimes (14.46) is quoted without proof or attribution, and the notion of an endless causal curve is not defined.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The logical dependence of the whole 3+1 split on a global causal assumption stays invisible.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Cite Geroch (1970) and the smooth-splitting refinement (Bernal and Sanchez 2003), and show a non-globally-hyperbolic example (anti-de Sitter or Minkowski with a point removed).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: §14.12 is dated and purely descriptive: it omits why raw ADM is numerically unstable (weak hyperbolicity), the BSSN and generalized-harmonic reformulations, moving-puncture gauges (1+log slicing, Gamma-driver shift), the 2005 binary black hole breakthrough, and gravitational-wave detections.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may believe the printed ADM system with maximal slicing is how modern codes work.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a short 'what changed' panel with the modern pipeline and a link to Baumgarte-Shapiro or Alcubierre's textbooks; keep the book's gauge menu as historical background.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Section 14.13 refers to 'the conformal approach of the last chapter', but that approach is in §14.12 of this chapter; the 2+2 claims (unconstrained data, ODEs along vector fields, Euler-Lagrange equations reproducing the dynamical equations) are asserted without derivation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusing pointer; the 2+2 advantages must be taken on trust.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Point to §14.12, and illustrate the null-data idea with a simple characteristic problem (the 1+1 wave equation on a double-null grid) before invoking 2+2 GR.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'If you were handed a snapshot of space at one instant, what would you need besides its shape to predict the future?' Steer toward the idea that you need how the shape is changing, which is the extrinsic curvature.

Start from surfaces in ordinary 3D space (a cylinder: intrinsically flat, extrinsically bent; a sphere: both) before introducing Lorentzian signs; then say that K for a slice plays the role of the second fundamental form.

Explain in the book's order but compress the calculations: projector, induced metric, induced derivative, K, then the curvature scorecard (Gauss/Codazzi/Ricci by number of normal indices), then constraints, then lapse, shift and evolution.

Keep a visible convention card throughout: signature (+,-,-,-), n.n = +1, gamma = -h, K = -(1/2) L_n h. Warn early that several printed equations mix h and gamma contractions, and give the (-,+,+,+) forms when the learner uses other sources.
Check for understanding: ask the learner to explain why the constraints contain no second time derivatives, and why the Ricci equation needs a family of slices rather than one.
Check for understanding: 'In flat Minkowski space with hyperboloidal slices, is K zero? Is (3)R zero? How can both be non-zero while spacetime is flat?' (Answer via the Gauss equation.)

For the lapse, have the learner derive N = d tau/dt themselves with one Taylor step, then connect to the Newtonian limit: N is roughly 1 + Phi, and A = -D ln N gives the acceleration needed to hover (sign per signature).

Use the lapse-shift triangle to derive the line element; then test with examples: Schwarzschild (N = sqrt(1-2M/r), zero shift), Painleve-Gullstrand (N = 1, flat slices, non-zero radial shift), rotating coordinates in flat space (shift = -Omega x r).

When the learner asks 'which equations do I solve?', lay out the pipeline: choose free data, solve 4 elliptic constraints, choose lapse and shift, evolve 12 first-order equations, monitor constraints.

Common question: 'Why not evolve lapse and shift too?' Answer: they are coordinate choices; in modern codes they are often given their own gauge-driver equations, but those are choices, not Einstein's equations.

Common question: 'Where are gravitational waves in these variables?' Use the degree-of-freedom count and point to the TT part of K and, in 2+2, the conformal 2-structure; tie to the two polarizations in Chapter 21.

Common question: 'Why is 3+1 bad for null infinity?' Explain that spacelike slices never reach null infinity and radiation travels along null directions, so characteristic (null) slicing is natural; preview Chapter 23.

For advanced learners, assign the component calculation of Exercise 14.4 (gamma and K for the spherically symmetric slice) and the verification of the 3+1 inverse metric by block multiplication; expect them to find the printed sign issues.
For novices, skip §14.5, §14.6 and §14.8 proofs; state the three equations with the scorecard picture and move to lapse, shift and the evolution idea.
